one_liner: Educational 100-line FP32 CUDA FlashAttention forward kernel; its 13x win over eager PyTorch attention is a cold-start profiling artifact.
what_it_does: A teaching re-implementation of the FlashAttention forward pass, with variable names taken from the paper, packaged as a PyTorch C++/CUDA extension that bench.py JIT-compiles with torch.utils.cpp_extension.load. You call minimal_attn.forward(q, k, v) on float32 CUDA tensors shaped [batch, heads, seq_len, head_dim] and get O back. There is no causal or padding mask, no dropout, no backward pass and no FP16/BF16, so it is not a replacement for F.scaled_dot_product_attention or flash-attn. A separate tensorcore branch adds a WMMA (TF32) kernel behind forward(q, k, v, use_tensor_cores).
how_it_is_fast: It applies FlashAttention-1 tiling with online softmax: K/V tiles of 32 rows and a Q tile go into shared memory, a running row max m and row sum l are kept, and partial outputs are rescaled, so the N x N score matrix is never written to global memory. The outer loop runs over K/V tiles and the inner loop over Q tiles (the FA1 order), so O, l and m are re-read and re-written in global memory for every K/V tile. There is one thread block of 32 threads per (batch, head), and each thread computes a whole query row's dot products serially on FP32 CUDA cores. That keeps the matmuls slow and occupancy low, so in practice it shows the I/O-aware idea rather than delivering speed. The tensorcore branch uses one warp per block with 16x16x8 TF32 WMMA fragments for QK^T and PV.
when_to_use: Learning how FlashAttention's tiling and online-softmax rescaling work, by reading about 100 lines of CUDA next to the paper's Algorithm 1.
A minimal starting point for your own attention-kernel experiments (many forks and open PRs add a backward pass, FA2 loop order, GQA or causal masking).
Classroom or interview exercises at small shapes (for example seq_len 64, head_dim 64, FP32) where correctness against a manual reference matters more than speed.
Checking a tensor-core rewrite step by step: the tensorcore branch keeps the naive kernel and a WMMA TF32 kernel side by side.
when_not_to_use: Any case where speed matters: measured with warm-up or CUDA events, eager PyTorch attention is faster (issues #11 and #13), and the README concedes it gets slower than the manual implementation for longer sequences and larger block sizes.
As a substitute for PyTorch SDPA, flash-attn or cuDNN attention: it was never benchmarked against them and runs FP32 one-thread-per-row matmuls without tensor cores (main branch).
Training, causal or masked attention, or FP16/BF16 models: forward only, no mask, FP32 inputs only (a BF16 request, issue #7, is open).
Sequence lengths that are not a multiple of the block size (32 on main, 16 in the tensorcore branch) or head dimensions above about 117 on main (see gotchas).
Code that relies on CUDA streams or multiple GPUs: kernels launch on the default stream, and the main branch queries shared memory on device 0 only.

integration.form: module (PyTorch C++/CUDA extension JIT-built from flash.cu and main.cpp by torch.utils.cpp_extension.load; the kernel can also be copied as a source-drop)
integration.min_toolchain: not documented (bench.py builds with nvcc -O2; the tensorcore branch sets TORCH_CUDA_ARCH_LIST=8.0 and -O3 -use_fast_math, and TF32 WMMA needs sm_80 or newer)
integration.platforms: NVIDIA GPUs with CUDA (README sample on a T4); the tensorcore branch targets Ampere (sm_80) or newer
integration.thread_safety: not documented; launches on the legacy default stream rather than PyTorch's current stream, and has no CUDA error checks

gotchas: The README speedup is not a speedup: bench.py profiles one cold call of each implementation (manual attention first) under torch.autograd.profiler with no warm-up, so the 52.5 ms baseline is mostly first-call initialisation; issue #16 adds that the old autograd profiler does not capture the custom op properly.

No bounds checks on N (derived from code): tiles are read and written in full for ceil(N/Bc) iterations, so a seq_len that is not a multiple of the block size reads past the head's slice and writes O out of range. A Faial data-race analysis (issue #1) found the main kernel race-free only when Bc == Br == blockDim.x, Tr <= blockDim.x and N >= blockDim.x^2.

Shared memory (derived from code, not tested): the main branch requests 3*Bc*d*4 + Bc*Br*4 bytes per block (28 KB at head_dim 64, 52 KB at 128) without the cudaFuncSetAttribute opt-in above the 48 KB default, and the launch is not error-checked, so head_dim above about 117 can fail without an error at the call and return the zero-initialised O. It also printf's the shared-memory line on every call.
The tensorcore branch cudaMallocs the l and m buffers on every call and never frees them (a leak of B*nh*N*8 bytes per call), and computes in TF32, which has less precision than the FP32 main kernel.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it only to read the algorithm in its smallest form. For a from-scratch learning path that ends at competitive speed, use the catalogued learn-cuda attention (gau-nernst, beats the flash-attn package on SM120) or Mini-Attention (beats cuDNN SDPA at short sequences). For real workloads, use FlashAttention-3/4 or cuDNN through PyTorch SDPA.
verified_claims_summary: The README's sample output on an AWS T4 is a single profiled forward call at batch 16, 12 heads, seq_len 64, head_dim 64, FP32: manual attention 52.545 ms vs minimal flash attention 3.908 ms Self CUDA time (about 13x, derived from page data), built with nvcc -O2, with CUDA and PyTorch versions not stated. The verifier judged this a cold-start artifact of timing an unwarmed baseline; warmed or CUDA-event-timed runs reported in issues #11 and #13 show eager PyTorch attention is faster.
status_note: Stale since 2024-12-30 (9 commits on main), and open PRs that add a backward pass, FA2 and GQA are unmerged; it is Apache-2.0 with 1.2k stars and is good teaching code, but not something to depend on for performance.
